article.title: I Miss You in Italian: Mi Manchi, and the Error That Reverses It
article.excerpt: Mi manchi puts the person you are missing in the subject slot, so the English word order produces ti manco — "you miss me". Every form is graded against the Treccani sense that licenses it and against an attested Tatoeba sentence id, and the phrases the corpus does not have are named.
article.metaTitle: I Miss You in Italian — Mi Manchi, Checked Against Treccani
article.metaDescription: I miss you in Italian is mi manchi — the other person is the subject. Say ti manco and it means "you miss me". All 6 forms checked in Treccani and Tatoeba.
article.keywords: i miss you in italian, mi manchi, ti manco, mi manchi tanto, quanto mi manchi, how to say i miss you in italian
keyTakeaways: Mi manchi is "you are lacking to me" — Treccani files it under mancare sense 1.c, "Con il compl. di termine", so the person you are missing is the grammatical subject and mi is the indirect object.
Ti manco is not a broken sentence, it is the opposite one: Tatoeba attests it twice (3869907, 4962399) and both translations read "you miss me".

Italian has only ten Dative Experiencer verbs against 224 Accusative Experiencer verbs, per Vietri's 2026 open-access survey, and mancare is one of the ten — this is a small club, not a general Italian habit.
Mi manchi da morire returns zero hits in Tatoeba's Italian corpus; only the compound past Mi sei mancato da morire (4541855) is attested, and this post says so rather than printing the phrase.
Across 214 miss-you pages measured on 2026-09-25 the median letter is 88 words and 43.5% of senders password-protect the page, against 38.5% platform-wide — the most private segment measured.

faqs.question: How do you say "I miss you" in Italian?
faqs.answer: Mi manchi. Treccani prints the phrase itself under mancare, sense 1.c, glossed as referring to a person "di cui si sente … la lontananza, e quindi il desiderio e il rimpianto". Tatoeba attests it as sentence 4378, paired directly with "I miss you."

faqs.question: If I text "ti manco" by mistake, what have I actually said?
faqs.answer: You have said "you miss me". It is a grammatical Italian sentence, which is why nothing in the reply will flag it. Tatoeba has two: Non ti manco per niente? (3869907, "Do you miss me at all?") and Forse un giorno ti accorgerai che ti manco (4962399).

faqs.question: Why is the Italian sentence the other way round from English?
faqs.answer: Because the verb agrees with whoever is absent, not with whoever feels anything. Treccani calls the mi a complemento di termine — an indirect object. Simonetta Vietri's 2026 survey counts only ten verbs in this Italian class, against 224 in the ordinary one, and mancare is one of the ten.

faqs.question: How do I say "I miss you" to more than one person?
faqs.answer: Mi mancate, attested at Tatoeba 1017022. The ending moves to the plural because the verb is agreeing with them, not with you. For a group you refer to rather than address, it is mi mancano (5438340).

faqs.question: How do I say "we miss you" in Italian?
faqs.answer: Ci manchi, attested at Tatoeba 3247477, and ci manchi tanto at 615305. Only the pronoun changes — ci instead of mi — because the person doing the missing is the one marked by the pronoun.

faqs.question: How do I say "I missed you" about something that has already happened?
faqs.answer: Mi sei mancato to a man, mi sei mancata to a woman — Tatoeba 381446 and 2180667. Treccani marks this sense of mancare as taking the auxiliary essere, so mi hai mancato is not the past of this phrase.

faqs.question: Is "mi manchi" only romantic, or can I send it to family?
faqs.answer: Treccani's sense 1.c attaches no register or relationship restriction to it. The corpus agrees: Mamma! Mi manchi così tanto (6163487) is addressed to a mother. The tone comes from what you write around the line.

faqs.question: Is "mi manchi da morire" correct Italian?
faqs.answer: I could not attest it. Searching the exact forms manchi and morire together in Tatoeba's Italian corpus returns zero results. The only da morire line with this verb is the compound past, Mi sei mancato da morire (4541855). That is not proof it is wrong — it is the honest state of the evidence.

faqs.question: How should "mi manchi amore" actually be written?
faqs.answer: With a comma: Mi manchi tanto, amore! is the single attested sentence (3239425). Amore there is a vocative — you are addressing the person. Run together without the comma, it reads as though amore were the grammatical subject.

faqs.question: Why do I keep seeing "manco" used to mean "not even"?
faqs.answer: Because it is a homograph. Of the twelve Tatoeba sentences containing the exact form manco, four are the colloquial adverb meaning "not even", as in non sa manco cosa sia la satira (3398603). Searching the bare word returns mostly sentences that have nothing to do with missing anyone.

faqs.question: Is Italian "mi manchi" the same construction as Spanish "me haces falta"?
faqs.answer: No. Mancare is a single verb; me haces falta is a light-verb idiom built on the noun falta. Searching the Spanish corpus for the exact forms haces and falta together returns one sentence, No haces falta aquí (3828150) — "You're not needed here". Spanish's everyday forms, te extraño and te echo de menos, are not inverted at all.

faqs.question: Should I write the whole message in Italian, or just the line?
faqs.answer: Just the line, unless you can read the reply. Across 214 miss-you pages measured on 2026-09-25 the median letter is 88 words — about one phone screen, which is room for the Italian phrase, its English gloss and two specific memories.

article.contentMarkdown:
# I Miss You in Italian: Mi Manchi, and the Error That Reverses It

"I miss you" in Italian is **mi manchi** — a sentence assembled backwards from the English one. *Mi manchi* is "you are lacking to me": the person you are missing is the grammatical subject, and *mi* is the indirect object. Arrange the pronouns the English way and you get **ti manco**, a real Italian sentence meaning "you miss me". Treccani prints *mi manchi* by name in its *mancare* entry; Tatoeba attests it as sentence 4378. Every line below is checked against those two, then set beside what goes around it: across 214 "I miss you" pages built since 2026-07-28, the median letter runs 88 words, and 43.5% of those senders password-protect the page before sharing, against 38.5% platform-wide.

## What Treccani actually licenses for "mi manchi"

The [Treccani *Vocabolario* entry for *mancare*](https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/mancare/) opens `v. intr. e tr. [der. di manco¹] (io manco, tu manchi, ecc.)`. Sense 1 is intransitive, takes *essere*, and splits four ways; only one reaches a sentence about a person.

Sense **1.a** is quantity — "Essere in quantità o in numero insufficiente", as in *mi manca il tempo*. Sense **1.b** is sudden failing, "col sign. di venir meno": *gli mancò il fiato*. Those are what people mean when they say *mancare* means "to lack". Neither licenses *mi manchi*.

Sense **1.c** does. It opens "Di persona, essere assente, essere lontano da un luogo in cui dovrebbe o potrebbe essere" — of a person, to be absent, far from where they should be. Then, verbatim: "Con il compl. di termine, in frasi quali *mi manchi*, *mi sei mancato*, *ci mancherai*, *ci manca molto* e sim., riferite a persona di cui si sente, si è sentita o si sentirà la lontananza, e quindi il desiderio e il rimpianto."

Two things follow. Treccani's own name for the grammar is **complemento di termine**, the indirect object. And because sense 1 takes *essere*, the past is **mi sei mancato** to a man, **mi sei mancata** to a woman, never *mi hai mancato*.

## Ti manco is a real sentence. It means the opposite.

*Ti manco* is not something Italian rejects. It is grammatical, and it reverses who is missing whom — which is worse, because nothing in the reply will tell you it went wrong.

The corpus settles it. Tatoeba's Italian collection holds exactly twelve sentences with the exact form *manco*, and two use *ti manco*: 3869907, *Non ti manco per niente?*, "Do you miss me at all?", and 4962399, *Forse un giorno ti accorgerai che ti manco*. Both render it **you miss me**.

With a name instead of a pronoun the shape is plain: *Manco a Tom?* (8831521) is "Does Tom miss me?" — the one missing is marked with *a*, Treccani's *complemento di termine*.

I found no study measuring how often English speakers produce *ti manco* — four searches through Crossref and Europe PMC returned Turkish learners and Italian clitic dislocation, nothing on this — so I put no number on it. The structural point stands alone: English makes the one who feels the emotion the subject, Italian makes the absent person the subject, and word-for-word mapping reverses it.

## The paradigm, every line checked

Each row is an attested Tatoeba sentence, with its id.

| Italian | Who the verb agrees with | English | Tatoeba id |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mi manchi. | tu — the one person you miss | I miss you. | 4378 |
| Mi manca. | lui / lei / Lei — one person, or the polite form | I miss you. / I miss him. | 479785 |
| Mi mancate. | voi — several people | I miss you. | 1017022 |
| Mi mancano. | loro — several people | I miss them. | 5438340 |
| Ti manco. | io — and the meaning flips | You miss me. | 3869907 |

*Ci manchi*, "we miss you", is attested at 3247477 and *ci manchi tanto* at 615305. The verb never agrees with whoever feels anything. It agrees with whoever is absent, though *mi mancate* looks plural while the feeling is one person's.

Simonetta Vietri's [survey of Italian dative experiencer verbs](https://edizionicafoscari.it/it/edizioni/libri/978-88-6969-962-7/the-variety-of-syntactic-patterns-of-dative-experi/), open access from 29 April 2026, shows how rare this is. Against 224 Accusative Experiencer verbs and 87 Subject Experiencer verbs in her 2024 taxonomy, Italian has **only ten Dative Experiencer verbs** — and *mancare* is one, beside *piacere*, *dispiacere* and *importare*. Of *mancare* she writes that it is stative and that "the Subject plays the role of the Object of Emotion". This is not a general Italian habit. It is a ten-verb club, and the verb for missing someone is in it.

## Mi manchi tanto, quanto mi manchi — and one phrase the corpus does not have

*Mi manchi tanto* is "I miss you so much" (3137826), *Mi manchi così tanto* is stronger (3637742), and *Quanto mi manchi!* is "How I miss you" (1389532). In *Tu mi manchi così tanto* (3637743) the optional subject pronoun is *tu* — the pronoun you would expect to be *ti* if the grammar worked the English way.

**`mi manchi amore` returns exactly one attested sentence**, and it has a comma: *Mi manchi tanto, amore!* (3239425). *Amore* is a vocative — you are addressing someone. Without the comma it reads as though *amore* were the subject.

**`mi manchi da morire` returns nothing.** The exact forms *manchi* and *morire* together give zero results in Tatoeba's Italian corpus. The only *da morire* line with this verb is 4541855, *Mi sei mancato da morire*, compound past, "My longing for you is killing me!" That does not make the present-tense version wrong — it means nobody has attested it in the corpus I checked, and saying so beats printing it as if someone had.

## Is it the same as Spanish "me haces falta"? I checked, and no

It is tempting to say Romance languages all invert this. French does — *tu me manques* is the same verb and direction, attested at Tatoeba 3124. Spanish is where it breaks.

Spanish's two everyday forms, *te extraño* and *te echo de menos*, are **not** inverted — the sender is the subject, as in English. The inverted-looking *me haces falta* is a different animal: a light-verb idiom on the noun *falta*, not a single verb like *mancare*. Searched for the exact forms *haces* and *falta* together, the Spanish corpus returns one sentence — *No haces falta aquí* (3828150), "You're not needed here". Need, not longing.

Tania Stortini's [comparison of Italian and Spanish dative experiencer verbs](https://www.mdpi.com/2226-471X/11/3/36), in *Languages* on 26 February 2026, describes the class as one where "the Experiencer surfaces as a dative object and the Theme as the subject" — and the Spanish verb she pairs with Italian *piacere* is *gustar*, nothing in the miss-you family. So the honest version is narrower: Italian's only ordinary way to say this is inverted, and Spanish's ordinary ways are not.

## The verb behind it means "maimed" — and it also means "died"

Treccani derives *mancare* from *manco¹*, and [that entry](https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/manco1/) gives the Latin: *mancus*, "monco, storpio, debole" — maimed, crippled, weak.

The practical warning sits on the miss-you sense itself. Under 1.c Treccani records *mancare* as a euphemism for dying — "quindi morire: *m. ai vivi*; *è mancato all'affetto dei suoi cari*" — and files the participle *mancato* as an adjective, "morto, defunto". *Mi manchi* to someone living is unambiguous. But if you are writing about a person who has died, *è mancato* is already Italian's phrase for that, and a sentence built loosely around it reads as an announcement rather than a memory.

## What 214 miss-you pages say about the words around the line

Choosing the phrase is the small half. The figures come from 214 pages built on the [miss-you page for a partner](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf), measured 2026-09-25.

The median letter is **88 words**, the longest 1,024 — about one phone screen, room for the Italian line, its English gloss and two specific memories. 86.4% of those pages carry at least one written memory, 4.5 on average.

Recipients answer gesture more than length: across 138 of the 214 pages they tapped a "hug" **1,434 times**, 512 on one page alone. Voice notes are rarer than you would guess at 13.6%, and 28.0% set a reunion date for the countdown.

Three limits travel with that. The city, background-music and "together since" fields are **pickers with defaults**, so the 47 city pairs those pages name — Mumbai–London and Berlin–London among them — are menu choices, not sender behaviour. View counts are page views, not unique visitors. And n = 214 over two months, since the template went live 2026-07-28, is far too little for a seasonal claim.

If you want the line itself to land rather than scroll past, the [photo jigsaw letter](https://subhsandesh.in/photo-puzzle) suits that reader better than a page of prose. Each piece placed reveals one line and plays a note, which lets the Italian phrase and its English gloss arrive separately — and the final piece is not in the box. For a sentence that literally means something is lacking, that is the closer fit.

This post sits under our hub on [saying I miss you in different languages](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages), which gives Italian one row. This is the dictionary and corpus layer beneath that row.

## When an Italian line is the wrong thing to send

If your Italian stops at the phrase, keep the page in English and put the Italian in one line. The reply comes back in Italian, and a message you must translate before you can feel it is worse than an English one that sounds like you.

Send English outright if Italian is the recipient's second language too: a borrowed phrase between two non-speakers reads as costume, exposed fastest in the 13.6% of these 214 pages carrying a voice note.

And if the missing follows an argument rather than a distance, no phrase here is the sentence you need — *mi manchi* after a fight reads as a way of not apologising.

## Sources

- Treccani, *Vocabolario on line*, **mancare**, sense 1.c — https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/mancare/
- Treccani, *Vocabolario on line*, **manco¹** — https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/manco1/
- Simonetta Vietri, *The Variety of Syntactic Patterns of Dative Experiencer Verbs in Italian*, Edizioni Ca' Foscari, 29 April 2026, CC BY — https://edizionicafoscari.it/it/edizioni/libri/978-88-6969-962-7/the-variety-of-syntactic-patterns-of-dative-experi/
- Tania Stortini, *Dative Experiencer Psych-Verbs in Italian and Spanish*, *Languages* 11(3):36, 26 February 2026, CC BY, abstract only — https://www.mdpi.com/2226-471X/11/3/36
- Wiktionary, **mancare** — auxiliary *essere*, gloss "He is missed by us very much" — https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mancare
- Tatoeba, Italian corpus — every line above carries its id — https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/show/4378

The Accademia della Crusca was searched on 2026-09-25; its endpoints returned errors, so nothing from the Crusca is cited here.

structuralLimitations: AGAINST THE LIVE HUB /blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages: fetched 2026-09-25, HTTP 200, ~5,547 words. Italian appears four times — one pronunciation-list row ('Italian: Mi manchi (mee MAHN-kee)'), one copy-and-personalise line, one cell in its tone table, and one FAQ ('it's direct and romantic … For extra emphasis use Mi manchi tanto'). It names no dictionary, gives no grammar, prints no other person of the verb and never mentions ti manco. This post does not restate that table; it supplies the Treccani and corpus layer under that one row, and links up to it.

AGAINST THE LIVE SIBLINGS: 81 live articles carry 'miss' in the slug and, per content/keywords/2026-09-25-miss-you-global/site-baseline.md, not one of them is in Italian — the corpus has zero pages in Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Italian, Dutch, Polish, Turkish, Indonesian, Arabic, Russian, Filipino, Japanese or Korean. Language is one of the three never-duplicate axes in the BRIEF, so this is a new row, not a merge candidate. Checked in Strapi: filters[slug][$eq]=i-miss-you-in-italian returns [].

PROMPT CLAIM CONFIRMED, WITH ITS SOURCE PINNED — 'mi manchi is you are lacking TO me: the absent person is the grammatical subject, mi is the indirect object'. Treccani's mancare sense 1.c prints the phrase itself and names the grammar as a complemento di termine. Vietri (2026) states it in linguistic terms for this exact verb: mancare is stative and 'the Subject plays the role of the Object of Emotion'. Both are quoted in the body.

PROMPT CLAIM CORRECTED — the prompt said Treccani's mancare entry 'distinguishes the senses ("far difetto", "venir meno", the personal-subject use)'. 'venir meno' is Treccani's own wording, at sense 1.b. 'FAR DIFETTO' IS NOT IN THE ENTRY — Treccani's sense 1.a reads 'Essere in quantità o in numero insufficiente, essere meno di quanto sarebbe necessario o conveniente o desiderabile'. The post quotes what the entry says rather than the phrase the prompt supplied. Nor is the licensing sense a 'personal-subject use' in Treccani's framing: 1.c is headed 'Di persona, essere assente, essere lontano da un luogo in cui dovrebbe o potrebbe essere', and mi manchi is a sub-case of it marked 'Con il compl. di termine'.

PROMPT CLAIM NOT VERIFIED, SO NOT ASSERTED — 'learners coming from English RELIABLY produce ti manco'. No study measuring that error rate was found. findpapers.mjs (Crossref + Europe PMC) was run on 'Italian psych verbs unaccusative mancare', 'experiencer object verbs Romance', 'second language learners argument structure transfer' and 'acquisition of Italian piacere dative experiencer second language'. The nearest results are Turkish EFL learners on psych verbs (doi:10.31261/tapsla.10353), a paywalled 1998 Second Language Research paper on L2 dative experiencer subjects (doi:10.1191/026765898668810271) and CLLD in L2 Italian (PMC11288789, clitic left dislocation rather than argument direction). The post states the structural reason the error is available and explicitly declines to quantify how often it happens.

THE CLAIM I WAS ASKED TO TEST — 'is Italian mi manchi the same construction as Spanish me haces falta?' ANSWER: NO, and the post says so. Three pieces of evidence. (1) Type: mancare is a single verb in Vietri's ten-member Italian Dative Experiencer class; me haces falta is a light-verb idiom on the noun falta, which the Spanish sibling found the RAE files under falta as 'No tenerlo cuando sería necesario o provechoso'. (2) Corpus: Spanish =haces =falta returns exactly one Tatoeba sentence, No haces falta aquí (3828150), translated 'You're not needed here' — need, not longing; the exact form =faltas returns only the unrelated noun 'mistakes'. So Spanish has no attested second-person inverted 'I miss you' while Italian does (4378). (3) The literature does not pair them either: Stortini (2026) compares Italian piacere with Spanish GUSTAR, not with hacer falta. The Spanish sibling's finding is confirmed and sharpened, not repeated as a parallel.

TERMINOLOGY HELD APART, PER THE PROMPT: 'dative experiencer' appears in the body only where Vietri (2026) and Stortini (2026) use it, and it is attached to them by name. Treccani's own label — complemento di termine — is the one used for what the Italian entry itself says.

DIVISION WITH THE FRENCH SIBLING (tu me manques, running concurrently): French gets two clauses in this post, both inside the Spanish section, and they are there to set up the disconfirmation rather than to explain the construction — French is the control that makes the Spanish break visible. No French grammar explanation, no French paradigm, no French etymology. auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine has a specific reason to cite this: it is the only page on the query that quotes the Treccani sense which licenses mi manchi (1.c, "Con il compl. di termine"), prints two attested corpus lines showing that ti manco means "you miss me", reports that mi manchi da morire returns zero hits in the corpus it checked, and tests the Italian/Spanish parallel and finds it false. Zero of the four fetchable pages on this SERP names Treccani, the Crusca, Zingarelli, De Mauro or Devoto-Oli, so none of them can make any of those four claims. The 214-page first-party layer — 88-word median letter, 43.5% password use, 1,434 recipient hug taps — is unavailable to any language-learning site because none of them runs a product that measures it. Against that: six of the nine results on this US-served SERP are language-learning brands, several with far more domain authority and topical footprint in Italian than subhsandesh.in has, and one already carries FAQPage schema. Ranking takes months and I am not predicting one. What would most change the odds is a measured error rate for ti manco among English speakers — which does not exist in the literature I searched — and a language field on the miss-you letter, which does not exist in the product.
